# Review pull requests with the Smithers action
https://smithers.sh/docs/guides/pr-review-action/

Get an agent review with a narrated HTML walkthrough on your pull requests, without running inference yourself.

`smithers review` runs one review agent per changed file, then a narrator agent writes a walkthrough of the whole change: chapters in logical reading order, prose explaining why each group of files changed, diffs embedded at the right point in the narrative, and Mermaid diagrams wherever structure changed. The output is a single self-contained HTML file you can open, share, or publish to a hosted URL.

Pointed at a GitHub pull request, it also posts the review onto the PR: the narrative summary as the review body, and every finding as an inline comment with a `suggestion` block when there is replacement code to apply.

Findings never fail the build. smithers review reports; humans decide.

## Before you start

- Register your repository. v0 accounts are operator-issued while billing is built out: open an issue titled `review access: <org>/<repo>` on [smithersai/smithers](https://github.com/smithersai/smithers/issues) or contact the maintainers.
- No secrets, no Anthropic account, no smithers checkout are needed. The service authenticates your repository through GitHub OIDC, runs the agents on its metered inference, posts the review, and hosts the walkthrough.

## 1. Add the workflow file

Create `.github/workflows/smithers-review.yml`:

```yaml
name: smithers review
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]

permissions:
  id-token: write       # proves your repo's identity to the review service
  contents: read        # check out the PR
  pull-requests: write  # post the review

concurrency:
  group: smithers-review-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.event.issue.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: smithersai/smithers/apps/review/action@main
```

The three permissions are the whole set the action needs: `id-token: write` proves your repository's identity to the review service, `contents: read` checks out the PR, and `pull-requests: write` posts the review.

:::caution
Keep the workflow on `pull_request`. Never switch it to `pull_request_target`: the review agents execute the PR's code, and `pull_request_target` would hand that code elevated credentials.
:::

## 2. Trigger a review

Comment on any pull request:

```text
@smithers review
```

Only owners, members, and collaborators can trigger reviews. Repositories registered in `auto` mode skip the comment and review every non-draft PR push; `comment` mode is the default. The mode is a server-side setting on your registration, so switching never touches your workflow file.

Subscriptions meter reviewed PRs as a monthly per-repo allotment, and the status comment shows remaining quota. Re-reviewing a PR that already counted this month is free. When the quota is spent, the action skips with a notice instead of failing your checks.

## 3. Pay for your own inference (optional)

To pay for the review's inference directly instead of using the service's metered inference, set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as a repository secret and pass it through in the job:

```yaml
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    env:
      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
    steps:
      - uses: smithersai/smithers/apps/review/action@main
```

`OPENAI_API_KEY` works the same way and moves both seats onto the `openai:` provider. The action prefers Anthropic when both are set, and it scrubs the raw secret out of the environment before the review starts: the run reads an untrusted diff, so it is handed only the credential its chosen mode needs. Repository registration, quota counting, and walkthrough hosting work exactly as before; only the inference moves to your key.

`CODEX_AUTH_JSON` and `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` are ignored. Those were the 0.x subscription modes; this release runs no CLI subprocess, so the credential is an API key and there is nothing to materialize on disk.

## 4. Run the same review from a terminal

`review` is not a Smithers engine verb. The review package ships its own bin, `smithers-review`, which runs the same flow against any repository on your machine:

```bash
# review the working tree of a repo, write .smithers-review/walkthrough.html
smithers-review /path/to/repo

# review a branch against main, open the walkthrough when done
smithers-review /path/to/repo --from main --to HEAD --open

# review one commit
smithers-review /path/to/repo --commit abc1234

# review GitHub PR #123 and post the review onto it (via gh)
smithers-review /path/to/repo --pr 123

# publish the walkthrough to the share service and print an unlisted URL
smithers-review /path/to/repo --pr 123 --publish

# no seats: deterministic story, no review findings (works offline)
smithers-review /path/to/repo --no-review --no-narrate
```

The repository path defaults to the current directory. `--publish` needs a publish service URL in `SMITHERS_REVIEW_PUBLISH_URL` and an operator-issued API key in `SMITHERS_REVIEW_PUBLISH_TOKEN`; both can also be set in `~/.smithers-review.json`.

## Configuration knobs

Seats are `provider:model` strings, and the provider ahead of the colon decides which credential is read:

| Variable | What it sets |
| --- | --- |
| `SMITHERS_REVIEW_SEAT` | Reviewing and verifying seat. Default `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5`. |
| `SMITHERS_REVIEW_CHEAP_SEAT` | Narrating and quizzing seat. Default `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5`. |
| `SMITHERS_REVIEW_VERIFY_SEAT` | Overrides the verifying seat alone. |
| `SMITHERS_REVIEW_NARRATE_SEAT` | Overrides the narrating seat alone. |
| `SMITHERS_REVIEW_QUIZ_SEAT` | Overrides the quizzing seat alone. |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Credential for `anthropic:` seats. |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | Credential for `openai:` seats. |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | Credential for `openrouter:` seats. |
| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | Sends `anthropic:` seats to a proxy origin instead of `api.anthropic.com`. |

The `quiz` action input, and `--quiz on` / `--quiz off` on the bin, control the reviewer quiz: a short set of multiple-choice questions a reviewer can answer only after reading the change. It auto-triggers when the assessed impact is high or critical, and the walkthrough lists the reasons behind the assessment. Nothing blocks a merge on the score.

## Verify it worked

Comment `@smithers review` on an open pull request. The action posts the narrative summary as the review body and every finding as an inline comment, the status comment shows remaining quota, and the service hosts the walkthrough HTML. Because findings never fail the build, a review full of findings still leaves the check green; a spent quota skips with a notice instead.

- [Model seats](/docs/guides/model-seats/): what a `provider:model` seat string declares.

# Durable execution
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/durable-execution/

A coding agent runs for hours, calls models, edits files, and waits on people. The process running it will eventually stop: a deploy, a kernel kill, a laptop lid. Durable execution is the property that none of this matters to the flow. Smithers gets that property from one mechanism, the journal, and every other feature in the engine is a way of writing to it or reading from it.

## The journal is the one mechanism

A flow is a typed program whose side effects are recorded in a journal as they happen. When the process dies, the next process reads the journal and continues where the record stops. Agents, approvals, retries, and time travel are not separate systems. Each is built on that record.

The journal is a logical write-ahead log over SQLite. Every lifecycle write takes the durable channel, `emitDurable`, which allocates its sequence and commits inside the write transaction before returning. A saturated telemetry queue may drop an event; a lifecycle event is never on that queue.

## One transaction per step

Committing a journal entry makes the entry durable, but a run's executable state lives in stores beside the journal: run rows, attempt rows, the step cache. `Journal.transact` closes that seam. The state projection and its `emitDurable` calls run in one transaction as savepoints, so the row and the lifecycle entry describing it either both commit or both roll back. That is what makes the journal an account of record rather than a best-effort echo, and it is what one transaction per step means.

Publication follows COMMIT. A subscriber never sees an entry that later rolls back, and a rolled-back producer identity stays re-emittable instead of deduplicating against a sequence that does not exist.

The transaction is held for its whole body, so only storage work belongs inside it: no flow bodies, no host calls, and no `flush`, which waits on the lossy writer and would deadlock against the open transaction. Nesting is a savepoint: an inner `transact` defers its settlements to the outermost commit.

## Two channels, two guarantees

The journal runs two channels with different promises. `emitLossy` is a bounded, non-blocking queue for telemetry and may answer `Dropped` under pressure. `emitDurable` is the lifecycle channel: it opens its own transaction inline, allocates the sequence inside it, and returns only after the row is committed, so the returned sequence is already durable. The two channels fail independently, and neither failure is permanent.

Readers choose the same trade-off. `changes` is a bounded sliding buffer, so a slow subscriber loses entries with no error and no gap signal. `stream` is the lossless follower: durable history first, then committed changes.

## Replay, defined precisely

Replay is deterministic re-derivation from the record. `Seq` is the canonical per-run replay order and replay reads `ORDER BY seq`. When a process re-drives a run, every step the journal already holds is served from its recorded outcome instead of re-executing, and the first step with no record is where real work resumes. Producer identity `(runId, sourceId, sourceSeq)` is unique in the database, so an exact retry of a recorded emission collapses to a `Duplicate` receipt rather than a second entry.

Because replay reads the record, the features that look like separate machinery are readers of it. Time travel replays the rows to fork a run at a frame or rewind it, and a read-only sync follower receives the same rows verbatim.

Replay is also idempotent at the write. Two emissions under one producer identity are the same event when their event type and their canonically encoded, redacted payload and meta match; a reused producer sequence carrying different content fails `idempotency_conflict`. A retried write cannot double the record, and a changed one cannot hide inside it.

## What durable execution is not

Durable execution is not a message queue. The journal records one run's own history in order; it does not route work between producers and consumers.

Durable execution is not a cache. The step cache is a separate store with its own admission rules, and a cache miss costs a re-execution, never a lost run.

Durable execution is not a backup. The journal rows are the primary state of the run, replayed verbatim to every consumer; nothing is restored from a secondary copy.

## Trade-offs and why

A crash before COMMIT loses the whole unit. Work that already ran, an action body for instance, re-executes on the next drive. Durability bounds the loss at the transaction boundary; it does not erase it.

No local transaction makes a remote effect atomic. A step that charged a card before the crash runs again on resume unless the integration carries an idempotency key, a fencing token, or a compensation.

Journal rows are permanent and replayed verbatim to sync followers and time-travel consumers, so redaction is enforced on write, the one point where it can still be enforced. Executable state in the run and attempt stores is deliberately not redacted: rewriting a field because its name resembles a credential would corrupt the resume data.

Smithers vendors Effect's workflow surface rather than depending on it, and diverges to be stricter and more cacheable: the caller chooses the execution id, step keys are content-addressed, and only infrastructure interrupts consume a retry policy. The pages on [execution IDs and ownership](/docs/concepts/ownership/), [content addressing](/docs/concepts/content-addressing/), and [retries and interruption](/docs/concepts/retries/) take each divergence in turn.

- [Time travel](/docs/concepts/time-travel/)

# Flows, actions, and plans
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/flows-actions-plans/

Everything you author in Smithers is one of three things. An action is the atom that does work. A flow is the composite that names atoms. A plan is the keyed action graph a flow body compiles to, known in full before the first action runs. The admission model for running work is plan, approve, run: the graph exists first, a person or a policy accepts its digest, and only then does a node execute.

## Actions are atoms

An action is schemas and a tag. `Action.make(tag, options)` is pure data: payload fields, success and error schemas, a tier, idempotency identity, an optional retry policy. The implementation attaches later and separately, as a layer:

```ts
const Compile = Action.make("example/Compile", {
  payload: { target: Schema.String },
  success: Schema.String,
  tier: "sealed"
})

const compileLayer = Compile.toLayer(({ target }) =>
  Effect.succeed(`${target}.js`)
)
```

Because the declaration carries no code, a plan can name an action whose implementation is wired up somewhere else entirely, and the interpreter reports `unresolved_action` when nothing was wired. Identity comes from what the action declares, not from where the implementation happened to be defined. `Action.makeSystem` is the declared form that mints no requirement, which is how the engine's own steps, `Sleep`, `WaitFor`, `HumanTask`, and `Poll`, ship implementations with the engine instead of pushing a layer obligation onto their callers.

## Flows are composites

A flow is payload and success schemas plus a required pure `body`. There is no `toLayer` on a flow: a flow carries a body and never a handler, and `Interpreter.layer(flow)` is what registers it with a runtime. A flow with nothing to plan is an action. `Flow.make` also accepts a `maxRounds` bound for trampoline lineages, which must be a positive safe integer.

The body names atoms instead of calling them. `Compile.call(payload)` inside a body does not run the compile; it records a node that stands for the compile. When a drive cannot proceed, `InterpreterError` says why with a stable code: `unresolved_action` for an action with no implementation wired up, `duplicate_node_id` for two nodes answering to one dispatch address, `incomplete_graph` for topology the build reported.

## The plan is known before the first action runs

`Graph.build` turns a body into the plan-time graph the interpreter drives, and building is a pure function of the declarations and the payload. The whole shape of a round is known before its first action runs. Branch arms are evaluated once, symbolically, so the exit condition and the handoff site are visible topology before anything executes. A graph the build reported diagnostics for is inspectable but deliberately not compilable, so an incomplete topology is reported rather than half-driven.

The persisted plan in `@smthrs/plan` is the keyed form of that graph. Each node's key is a function of what the node consumes, and the plan digest covers node identity, every computed key, the edge set, and the declared effects. A plan grows by append and is never rewritten. `baseDigest` is the digest at generation 0, what a human approved and what a running run pins, while `digest` advances with each appended elaboration.

Planning performs no I/O. Declared effects carry read and write paths, never digests, because measuring a path is run-time work. The plan says what may touch what; the host says what is actually there.

## What the build refuses

Planning fails rather than guess. Building refuses a nesting depth past its bound and refuses a duplicate node id, because a node id is durable dispatch identity and two nodes answering to one address would let a later settlement overwrite an earlier one. `Plan.compile` refuses a cycle in the material dependencies, a reference to a node that is neither in the drafts nor already in the plan, and a write-set overlap under a `fail` verdict. The refusal codes are a closed set, so a new refusal is a deliberate addition, not a new free-form string.

## Plans are append-only

Recording is first-writer-wins: an identical re-record is not an error, and a different plan under the same id is a `Conflict` carrying the stored digest, never a silent overwrite. Append-only is enforced in SQL, not by convention: triggers raise on any update or delete of the node and edge rows and on any backward move of a plan row. Re-ordering after a reconciliation happens by re-keying future steps, never by rewriting recorded ones.

## Why bodies are planned, not executed inline

Static topology is what makes approval meaningful: there is a complete artifact to approve. It is what makes replay cheap: a re-driven body rebuilds the same graph and serves its recorded nodes from the journal. And it is what keeps the walk honest: the interpreter walks demand-driven from the root, because executing a branch arm to discover it was not taken is exactly what static topology exists to avoid.

The cost is a discipline on the author. A planned value may never be computed on: the type is branded, and the proxy traps throw rather than let a plan be built around `NaN` or `"[object Object]"`. A payload is stored as its inert JSON mirror. And a plan is always a DAG: there is no loop node, and repetition lives one level up, in what a flow settles with.

- [Module flows guide](/docs/guides/module-flows/)
- [`@smthrs/flow` reference](/docs/reference/api/flow/)
- [`@smthrs/plan` reference](/docs/reference/api/plan/)

# Content addressing
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/content-addressing/

A durable engine faces an identity question on every step: when this run resumes, which recorded result belongs to this step? Effect's own workflow package answers with the activity's name, so renaming an activity corrupts replay: the resumed run asks for a name nothing was recorded under. Smithers answers with content. A step is keyed by what it is, not by what it is called.

## Keys are derived from canonical content

A key is derived in three fixed steps: encode the input with `@smthrs/canonical` (RFC 8785 canonical JSON), hash the canonical UTF-8 document with SHA-256, and prefix the lowercase digest with `key1_`:

```ts
const key = await Effect.runPromise(
  deriveKey({ domain: "example/compile", version: 1, input: "main.ts" }).pipe(
    Effect.provide(NodeCrypto.layer)
  )
)
// key1_<64 lowercase hex>
```

Canonicalization is what makes the hash meaningful across hosts and across time: object keys sort, so two hosts that build the same content derive the same key. Decoding fails rather than approximates. A value carrying a lone surrogate, a non-finite number, or a cycle has no canonical form, and a best-effort string would produce a digest that silently disagrees with another host's.

## What folds into a step key

A call node's key material folds the declared schemas of the callee as their JSON Schema documents, so a change to what a callee accepts or produces re-keys the call. A plan node's key is a function of what the node consumes: an edited declaration re-keys that node and its dependent cone, and nothing else. Structural names are lookup addresses only and never enter the hashed value, so renaming an action or a node re-keys nothing.

The reference itself is hashed with its tag, so a pending reference and a resolved reference to the same dependency cannot collide. A dependency digest is resolved as an own property, so a reference naming `toString` or `constructor` is a refusal, not a colliding key.

That is the entire invalidation mechanism. There is no reverse-dependency index and no invalidating node visitor, because content addressing subsumes both.

## Sealed content keys and run-local ordinals

Only `sealed` material may become a content key. Compensable, irreversible, or unsealed work gets an ordinal key instead, which is deliberately run-local. The difference decides what a cache may do with the record: only a content-key record has an address another run can reproduce, so cross-run reuse exists only for sealed steps, and an ordinal-key record remains visible inside its own run and nowhere else.

## Namespaces keep identities apart

Callers own their domain material. A key input carries a stable domain and a material-schema version, for example `{ domain: "engine/action", version: 1, ... }`, whenever two protocols must not share an identity namespace. The runtime's own facts are namespaced the same way: the environment a sealed key is computed under is hashed separately from caller-owned identity, so caller declarations and environment layers can never alias each other.

## The stated limit

Key identity is JSON-Schema-shaped, and the limit is worth stating exactly: two schemas whose decoders disagree can serialize to the same JSON Schema document. Changing only a codec's behavior does not re-key the call, and a result recorded under the old codec replays under the new one. Effect codecs are not serializable, so nothing can close this automatically. An author who changes a transformation and needs the call re-keyed renames the declaration.

A plan diff's attribution, which fields changed, is a report for a human comparing declarations field by field, and it is deliberately part of no digest.

## Boundaries and trade-offs

A key is opaque. Only `@smthrs/keys` owns the `key<n>_` wire form, and `StoredKey` is the union of representations this release supports; `key2_` is invalid until a complete version-two contract exists. Parsing a stored key validates the exact text and needs no crypto service, so a key crossing persistence, RPC, or journal boundaries is checked without deriving anything.

Derivation fails with `KeyDerivationError` carrying a stable code: `canonicalization_failed` when the input has no accepted canonical form, `digest_failed` when the injected hash operation fails. Deriving a key is one-shot and holds the input, the canonical document, and the hash snapshot in memory, so an external boundary imposes its own size limits before derivation.

Canonicalization inherits JSON's erasures: negative zero canonicalizes as zero, an undefined object member is omitted, and an undefined array element canonicalizes as null. A distinction that matters to identity has to be encoded explicitly.

Content addressing trades a rename's convenience for replay's integrity. Keying on content means a stale result can never be served under a fresh declaration; it also means a refactor that changes payloads re-executes steps a name-keyed system would have served. The engine chooses re-execution, because a wrong replay is silent and a re-execution is visible.

- [`@smthrs/canonical` reference](/docs/reference/api/canonical/)
- [`@smthrs/keys` reference](/docs/reference/api/keys/)

# Execution IDs and ownership
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/ownership/

Two identity questions decide whether a durable run is safe: which run is this, and which process may mutate it. Smithers answers the first by letting the caller choose the execution id, and the second with a fence that follows the run's recorded owner. Effect's own workflow package answers the first by hashing the flow tag and payload, and Smithers refused that design.

## The caller chooses the execution id

Identity has three sources, consulted in a fixed order. First, the `executionId` the caller named on `execute`. Failing that, the `idempotencyKey` the flow declared, hashed together with the flow tag. Failing both, the ambient `CurrentExecutionIds` source, whose default `derived` hashes the flow tag with the payload's canonical form.

`layerExecutionIds(source)` replaces the third. Replace it when two equal payloads of one flow are not one piece of work in this host, for example one request per user in a coding agent. Callers that name an `executionId` and flows that declare an `idempotencyKey` are unaffected, because both are decided before the source is consulted.

`ExecutionIdRequired` is a defect, not a typed failure. The derived source raises it when the payload has no canonical form, a non-finite number, a lone surrogate, or a cycle, and `derived.mint` dies with it rather than starting a run under a guessed identity. `Flow.executionId(payload)` likewise dies when the payload fails the flow's own payload schema, where `Flow.execute` fails with a typed `SchemaError` instead. Precompute an id with `executionId` only for a payload you have already validated.

## Why the hash-everything join was refused

Upstream derives a run's identity by hashing the flow tag and payload, so two unrelated runs with equal payloads silently join: the second caller's run is the first caller's run, and each reads the other's history as its own. A silent join is worse than a crash, because nothing reports it. In Smithers the caller chooses the id, derivation is opt-in, and a flow with neither an explicit id nor a declared key dies with a structured defect instead of guessing.

## Fenced ownership

Every running run has an owner, an `OwnerId` of host id, process id, and nonce. Every ownership mutation compares all three fields in the same SQL statement as the mutation, so a claim, a heartbeat, an attempt write, or a terminal transition lands only while `flows_runs` still records that owner.

The journal carries the same fence. Attempt lifecycle writes pass the owner and append only while the persisted ownership matches; otherwise they fail `fence_lost`. An owner that is missing or malformed fails `invalid_event` instead: that is a caller contract violation, and reporting it as `fence_lost` would send the caller hunting a race that never happened. `OwnerId` lives in the journal package rather than with the arbitration in `@smthrs/run-store`, because the journal is what it fences.

## The claim protocol

A run row begins pending. Claiming is two phase, `claim` then `activate`, or atomic, `claimAndOwn`. The compare-and-swap reads a complete snapshot: status, owner, and heartbeat together. Partial ownership snapshots are invalid by construction, so a running row always carries both an owner and a heartbeat and every other status carries neither. Terminal rows cannot be reopened.

Compare-and-swap competition is reported as tagged success values such as `FenceLost` and `SnapshotChanged`, separate from the typed error channel, so a caller retries contention without treating corruption as a race.

Attempts sit under the same discipline. An attempt row is addressed by `(runId, stepKeyDigest, attempt)`, and its writes, `put`, `heartbeat`, `finish`, and `patch`, are fenced against the owning running run. `transitionOwned` changes status and optional executable state under one owner fence, with its optional cancellation guard compiled into the same update, so a cancel request cannot land between a check and a terminal write.

## The journal says which answer was used

Arbitration is auditable because the decision is journaled. A refused takeover records `steal-refused-owner-alive` with the evidence that refused it, `lease-fresh` when the lease was still inside the window or `probe` when a supplied liveness check answered for the owner. A takeover records `stolen-and-activated` with its evidence kind. A refusal is journaled once per lease and evidence, not once per sweep tick, because first-writer admission collapses every repeat about an unchanged lease into the one record.

A refusal also defers the run for two heartbeat ticks, doubling per consecutive refusal against the same lease, so the stale-run sweep keeps advancing past recently refused rows instead of re-probing them every tick.

## Zombie owners interrupt themselves

A process killed with SIGKILL leaves its runs marked `running` under a dead owner. A fresh process reclaims them through the lease: the default liveness check counts an owner as alive while its persisted heartbeat is younger than the staleness cutoff, and a steal re-checks the evidence against the row inside the same write, so a claimant that lies about the lease loses the compare-and-swap. The driver's periodic sweep re-drives the stale-running rows a hard-killed owner leaves behind, so neither SIGKILL nor an out-of-memory kill can strand a run.

The reclaimed owner is the zombie, and the fence is what stops it. When the old process wakes and tries to append its next attempt event, the fence fails the write with `fence_lost` and the zombie self-interrupts instead of appending. Ownership is observed at the write, not assumed from the claim.

## Trade-offs and why

Ownership is an arbitration protocol, not a lock manager. Evidence binds to one instant by exact equality, so a probe taken at T is refused by a call made at T+1. A deployment that knows more about liveness, a pid probe on the owner's host or an orchestrator's pod status, supplies its own `isAlive` check and refuses takeovers for longer; a pid names a process only in its own host's namespace, so cross-host recovery relies on the persisted lease.

Clocks get the same distrust. Lease operations refuse a caller clock reading that runs ahead of the store's clock by more than the skew allowance, so a runaway clock can neither steal a fresh owner nor pin a lease past the cutoff. Heartbeats are monotonic: a pulse delayed past a newer one is acknowledged without moving the lease backwards. A run row carries stamps from two clock sources, the caller's `nowMs` on lease operations and the Effect `Clock` on lifecycle transitions, and a composition must give both sources the same reading.

The fence is not a distributed lock. It arbitrates writes to one store, and it does nothing about a process that writes around the store. Ownership is not identity either: one caller may own many runs, and one run changes owners over its life as claims, steals, and recoveries accumulate.

# Retries and interruption
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/retries/

A durable engine cannot keep retry state in a fiber: the fiber dies with the process, and the retry has to outlive it. Smithers therefore treats a retry policy as data, treats cancellation as final, and reserves automatic retry for one explicitly marked class of interrupt.

## A retry policy is a plain value

A `RetryPolicy` is a frozen value: `initialMs`, `factor`, `maxMs`, `maxAttempts`, `expirationMs`, `jitterRatio`, and the `nonRetryable` tags. `RetryPolicy.make` validates the bounds and throws a `RangeError` naming the field that is wrong, and it copies and freezes the `nonRetryable` array so a later mutation of the caller's array cannot change what a parked policy means.

| Field          | Bound                                  |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `initialMs`    | finite and not negative                |
| `factor`       | finite and positive                    |
| `maxMs`        | finite and not below `initialMs`       |
| `maxAttempts`  | a safe integer of at least one         |
| `expirationMs` | finite and positive                    |
| `jitterRatio`  | finite, between zero and one inclusive |

The next delay is derived from a persisted attempt count, not from fiber-local `Schedule` state. `nextDelay` mirrors Temporal's `ComputeNextDelay` and is total even for a policy decoded from a persisted row: a non-finite attempt, elapsed time, bound, or computed delay answers `None` rather than handing the engine a negative or `NaN` duration to sleep. `decide` is the engine's single retry decision point, and non-retryable classification happens there and nowhere else: by the policy's declared tags, and by `defaultNonRetryable`, the integrity verdicts that must reach the driver unretried under every policy.

Because the decision reads durable state, retry deadlines survive restarts. A policy whose `expirationMs` elapsed while the process was down is already expired when the run resumes. Inside a body, `Action.retry` is Effect retry with durable attempt context, and `CurrentAttempt` exposes the one-based durable attempt, so every attempt of one retry sequence reuses its own action's ordinals.

## Cancellation propagates at once

Effect's own workflow package retries any interruption ten times by default. Smithers diverges on purpose: cancellation propagates at once. A cancel is a statement about the run, not an accident of the network, and retrying it would redo work the caller already refused. Durable cancellation is observed, not only recorded: while a run executes, the driver polls the run's cancel-requested flag on the heartbeat cadence and interrupts the flow fiber, and terminal transitions are guarded inside the ownership compare-and-swap, so a request that races past the last poll turns finalize into a cancellation. A cancel requested against a parked run is re-driven by the periodic sweep, so parking does not hide a run from its caller's refusal.

## Only infrastructure interrupts consume a policy

An interrupt marked `InfraInterrupt` means the host was lost or the work was rebalanced, not that the work failed. Only that marker is retried, and only under the action's `interruptRetryPolicy`. An exhausted `interruptRetryPolicy` dies with the typed `InfraInterruptRetriesExhausted`, carrying the action, the attempts, and the final interrupt.

A policy that runs out of road ends one of two ways, each a terminal failure with a stable code: `RetryPolicyExpired` when the deadline passed, and `RetryAttemptsExhausted` when the attempt budget did.

## A recorded failure replays as itself

Retry state survives the process because it is ordinary durable state. The attempt counter resumes from the persisted sequence, and a persisted `failed` attempt row replays by rethrowing the persisted domain failure, never by readmitting the step. The failure was schema-encoded before persistence, so its `_tag` survives the JSON round trip and the policy's non-retryable matching applies on replay exactly as it applied live. A crash cannot turn a settled failure back into running work, and a restart cannot reset the budget. Readmission refuses only a genuinely mid-flight row, one still marked `running`.

## Tiers bound what may be retried

Every action declares a tier. `sealed` work is deterministic and cacheable. `compensable` work can be undone. `irreversible` work permits neither: a payment, a post. An irreversible action may be retried only with a declared idempotency key, because retrying an unkeyed irreversible effect is how a charge happens twice; attempting it fails with `IrreversibleRetryRequiresIdempotencyKey`.

Ordinal-keyed work is serialized for the same reason. `ConcurrentKeylessDispatch` refuses two live dispatches of one keyless allocation scope, because arrival order would otherwise assign the ordinals the attempts replay under.

## Boundaries and trade-offs

A retry policy is not a schedule. It answers one question, how long until the next attempt and whether there is one, and it holds no state of its own.

An infrastructure interrupt is not a domain failure. A domain failure is recorded and replayed as itself; an infrastructure interrupt is evidence about the host, and it is the only thing a retry policy may consume.

The trade-off is deliberateness over coverage. Upstream's default retries everything and so retries cancels; Smithers retries nothing by default, so an author must declare which interrupts are infrastructure. The cost is annotation. The benefit is that a cancel is honored at once, and every retried step is a step someone marked as safe to redo.

# Capabilities and the host kernel
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/kernel/

A flow that edits files, spawns processes, and calls models holds real authority over the host it runs on. The kernel question is who granted that authority. Smithers answers with a closed list of host services, a closed vocabulary of capabilities over them, and a grant check on every call, so no flow reaches the host ambiently.

## The closed host surface

The host surface is a fixed list: `FileSystem`, `HttpClient`, `CommandLine`, `ChildProcessSpawner`, `Workspace`, and `Jj`. Each is a service a platform adapter supplies, and the kernel decorates the same tags with middleware layers. There is no second protected tag: composing a decorator over a raw host layer shadows that raw implementation for every consumer of the original tag, so a flow cannot walk past the check by importing the platform service directly. `Path` is pure manipulation and passes through unchecked.

`HostServices.layer` composes the closed protected surface at the application boundary, in one direction: the raw platform service, then the kernel decorator consulting the grant store, then the flow-visible service.

## The capability vocabulary

`Capability.Action` is the closed vocabulary: `fs:read`, `fs:write`, `net:get`, `net:post`, `model:call`, `proc:spawn`, and the jj slots `jj:status`, `jj:diff`, `jj:snapshot`, `jj:restore`, `jj:workspace-add`, `jj:workspace-forget`, `jj:root`, and `jj:revert`. Actions are durable identity: never repurpose one, add one. A capability carries an exact resource; a `CapabilityPattern` carries a glob matched byte-exactly against the whole resource.

`CapabilitySet` supplies the ambient authority ceiling, and its public operations can only preserve or narrow authority. Capability sets are monotone: a step can declare less than its enclosing flow, never more. Rules are ordered and last-match-wins, except that an effective configured deny is a hard veto, and the default decision is `ask`.

The vocabulary is tiered with the same tiers the action model uses. `Capability.tierOf` classifies a capability as `sealed`, `compensable`, or `irreversible`: reads are sealed, undoable writes are compensable, and the rest, a `net:post`, a `proc:spawn`, an `fs:write` that escapes the workspace, are irreversible. Only the irreversible ones require an idempotency key to retry.

The pattern grammar has no escape: a resource that genuinely contains `*` or `?` cannot be granted exactly. Patterns are derived from a concrete capability with `Capability.patternFromCapability`, never built by concatenating agent-supplied text.

## Grants and the grant store

A grant is a recorded decision. `GrantStore` resolutions are `once`, `run`, `remembered`, and `deny`. An attended store suspends the asking fiber on its request until a person answers; an unattended store fails immediately with `PermissionRequired`. `JournalGrantStore` persists a decision before activating it, so a `remembered` grant survives the process, and a persistence failure leaves the decision inactive. Replay accepts only the configured producer and known event types, and a policy history past the rule ceiling fails closed. Envelope patterns are treated as a set, deduplicated and sorted under a canonical signature over plan, scope, and pattern set, so one envelope is never persisted twice.

## What a grant names

The resource is chosen so a grant cannot be read wider than it was meant. GET and HEAD requests check as `net:get` and every other method as `net:post`. For an `https:` URL the resource is the lowercased URL host; for any other scheme it is the scheme plus the host, so a grant for a host never authorizes a cleartext `http` downgrade to it. Redirects are followed above the guard, so every hop re-enters authorization independently.

A spawn checks as `proc:spawn` with the rendered command line as its resource, and the grant identity is that line alone. The working directory and environment overrides are not part of what a grant authorizes; they reach an attended surface as display metadata only. A model call inside `HttpClient.withModelCall` checks as `model:call` with the model id appended to the resource, so a grant for one model says nothing about another.

## Checked paths stay checked

A checked pathname is not handed unchanged to a path-based host. Before the grant check, the kernel resolves every existing ancestor of the path and maps a canonical path inside the workspace back to the stable logical workspace root. After any grant suspension it resolves the resource again and refuses the operation if the path now names something else, and an open handle binds its authorization to the descriptor's device and inode identity, rechecked on guarded operations. An attended grant cannot be raced by swapping the file while the person is deciding.

## Cancelling a run leaves no process behind

The containment layer rewrites each spawned command to request `SIGTERM` and then `SIGKILL` after a grace period, and records every successful spawn in a ledger that is released when its scope closes. The ledger's durable records are replayed by the next incarnation of the same host, which obtains the orphans a dead owner left and reaps one only after verifying the record names a separate process group, the owner is gone, and the record belongs to the current boot.

## Typed permission failures

The failures are part of the contract: `PermissionRequired`, `PermissionDenied`, and `GrantStoreError`, with the stable codes `permission_required` and `permission_denied`. Effect owns the `FileSystem` and `ChildProcessSpawner` error channels, so the decorator projects its failure into `PlatformError` with the structured value on `cause`, where `Permission.fromPlatformError` recovers it. `Jj` owns its interface and names `PermissionError` directly.

A permission failure is journal-safe by construction: the capability is defensively copied and the metadata snapshotted at the construction site, so a value the journal could not encode fails there, not later at the persistence boundary.

## Why grant-checked, not ambient

Ambient authority asks nothing, which is exactly the problem: any code holding the service tag could reach the host, and nothing could say later why an operation was allowed. A grant check at the adapter call site makes authority explicit, attributable, and replayable. The journal holds the decision, the suspended fiber means the answer can take as long as a person needs, and mutable inputs are snapshotted so the operation executed after an attended grant is the operation that was authorized.

The boundary is honest about its limit. The kernel checks capabilities at adapter call sites; it does not sandbox the operating system and cannot observe host access that bypasses the decorated services. Hermetic execution additionally requires a `StepBoundary`. `GrantStore.makeNoop` is an explicit allow-all seam for tests, not a production policy. What the kernel guarantees is narrower and real: every access through the declared surface was granted, and the grant is on the record.

# Time travel
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/time-travel/

A finished run leaves a complete, ordered record of everything it did: every step, every attempt, every model call, keyed and sequenced. Because that record is complete, later programs can read it for answers and derive further work from it. `@smthrs/time-travel` is the package of protocols that do both. It exposes one service, `TimeTravel`, with four operations, each addressed by a `Position`: a run id plus a frame.

```ts




const program = Effect.gen(function*() {
  const timeTravel = yield* TimeTravel
  const lineageId = Engine.FlowEngine.Lineage.root("build-42")
  const position = { runId: "build-42", frame: { lineageId, seq: 17 } }
  return yield* timeTravel.inspect(position, { initial: 0, reduce: (state) => state + 1 })
})
```

A frame is `{ lineageId, seq }`: a sequence number on one lineage of the journal. Forks create descendant lineages, so the lineage id is part of the address, and `seq: 17` names the committed prefix through entry 17 of it.

## Replay reads and never executes

`replay` folds the committed journal prefix up to the frame through a pure projection you supply, and `inspect` is the same fold under the service defaults. The fold has no dispatcher, so a replay can never re-execute a model call or a child flow. That absence is what separates replay from an engine resume. Replay is always safe: it writes nothing, it streams, and it stops reading at the frame.

## Fork drives a copy

`fork` mints and reserves a child run id, provisions a jj workspace pinned at the frame's recorded pointer, copies the journal prefix and the attempts that prefix can explain, and records the lineage edge. The child is a real run you drive from the frame; the parent is never mutated. A fork refuses `live_parent` while the parent or any ancestor is live, because a live run has no settled prefix to copy. Forking one frame twice yields two independent child runs in two workspace lanes.

## Rewind re-derives a view

`rewind` removes the journal suffix after the frame so the run's state can be re-derived from that point. It validates the position before anything durable exists, claims the run and holds the ownership lease with a heartbeat, writes an audit row, assesses every effect boundary in the suffix, compensates what can be undone, restores the jj workspace to the frame's pointer, and archives and truncates the suffix atomically. A descendant still depending on the truncated history refuses the rewind with `live_child` under the default `detachedChildren: "block"` policy. The `"cancel"` policy cancels detached children only after the truncation commits, because cancellation is terminal and has no inverse.

## Compensation undoes within declared boundaries

Effects in the truncated range are undone by the `CompensationHandlers` you register, and a handler is held to recorded evidence: an effect that recorded a compensation descriptor resolves only to the handler declaring the same one, so an adapter swapped in after a restart never compensates evidence another implementation left behind. With no handlers provided, a crossed record that is not sealed classifies as blocking and the rewind fails `irreversible`. That is the safe default: the protocol stops rather than leave the world half reverted.

## Recovery heals a wedged run

Recovery is not an operation. Building `TimeTravel.layer` finishes or rolls back every rewind a crash interrupted, before the service accepts work. The one audit it declines is one whose run a live process still holds: that audit stays pending and a later build finishes it, so recovery never steals a run from a living owner.

## Boundaries

Time travel is not editing history. Nothing rewrites a committed entry in place: a rewind moves the suffix after the frame into an archive and records an audit row for the whole operation, so the evidence of what the run did survives its truncation. Replay is not a resume: nothing re-executes, and a coordinate the journal does not hold is a `not_found`, not a re-run. Compensation is not a general undo: it covers exactly the effects your handlers declare, within the boundaries the journal recorded. In 1.0.0-rc.0 time travel is a library API only: there is no CLI verb, and the matching MCP tools answer with the `unsupported` envelope.

## Failure answers

Every operation fails as a `TimeTravelError` discriminated by a closed `code`, so a caller's branch stays exhaustive: `busy` when another owner holds the run, `live_parent` and `live_child` for the ancestry refusals, `irreversible` when an effect in the truncated range cannot be undone, `rate_limited` when the supplied limiter rejects the attempt, `limit_exceeded` when the history cap is reached, and `invalid` or `not_found` for coordinates that address nothing. An error never attaches a whole effect record: a blocking assessment travels as its identity and classification, never as the effect's input or output.

## Limits and why they exist

Every read is capped by `maxHistoryEntries` (default 100,000), so one call's cost is bounded rather than a function of the journal's length; `pageSize` is a throughput knob and never changes a derived answer. The durable store is the SQLite dialect only. The engine is the producer of everything the service reads: anchors reach the snapshot tables through a projection of journal records, so the engine never writes this package's tables and the dependency arrow stays one way.

## Related

- [Durable execution](/docs/concepts/durable-execution/): the journal mechanism every time-travel verb reads.
- [Compensation](/docs/guides/compensation/): declare the rollback handlers a rewind calls.
- [Time travel tutorial](/docs/tutorials/time-travel/): walk a fork and a rewind end to end.

# Sync and read-only followers
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/sync/

Everything a run has done is in its journal. A second process that wants to watch runs does not need authority over them; it needs the journal stream. `@smthrs/sync` is read-only journal replication: a server that pages and streams journal entries, and a client that follows one run or a whole workspace from durable cursors.

```ts



const scope = Schema.decodeUnknownSync(SyncProtocol.RunScope)({
  _tag: "Run",
  runId: "build-42"
})
const cursor = Schema.decodeUnknownSync(SyncProtocol.RunCursor)({
  runId: "build-42",
  afterSeq: 17
})
```

## The wire

The protocol is two RPCs. `Sync.Read` answers one bounded page of entries for a scope and a cursor set. `Sync.Subscribe` streams `Entries` frames, each carrying one run's entries and the interval the server covered, until the credit the request paid runs out or the server closes the stream. Credit is a hard limit on frames, not a sliding acknowledgement window: there is no Ack RPC, and a follower that wants more resubscribes from the cursors it has acknowledged. A cursor is per run and means "entries after this sequence"; journal sequences may have holes, so the next entry is not required to be exactly one greater.

A read stops at the first of three bounds: the request's `limit`, the frame ceiling, or the durable tail of every covered run, which is the only case that reports `done: true`. `RunCatalog` supplies the run list for a workspace read, and a workspace subscription reconciles the runs it covers against that list on every round, so a run created mid-follow joins the stream and a dropped notification costs latency, never state.

## What a follower can do

A follower projects the journal into whatever read model it needs: a dashboard, an audit trail, a search index, a materialized view of run state. It inspects any run its credential covers, catching up through `Sync.Read` until the server reports done and then following live through `Sync.Subscribe`. `SubscribeOptions.apply` upgrades a cursor from delivered to applied: the callback runs to success before the cursor moves, so a consumer whose own write fails re-receives the entry instead of skipping it. A lost transport reconnects under exponential backoff capped at five seconds, resuming from the acknowledged cursors. When compaction deletes entries below a cursor, the client moves that run's cursor to the checkpoint and restarts the subscription, and `SubscribeOptions.onResync` runs before the move and must succeed, so nothing is skipped silently.

## What a follower never does

A follower never writes. The wire carries no submission path: client-to-server commands are `BranchRpcs`, which has no production mount at 1.0.0-rc.0, so the gateway serves `SyncRpcs` alone. A follower never claims a run and never resumes one. Ownership stays with engines, and a follower holds no lease, no fence, and no dispatcher. Sync is not a control channel: steering and approvals belong to the control plane, not the journal feed.

## Principals and authorization

Every request is answered against a principal, and the default is anonymous. Over RPC, `SyncAuth.layer` establishes the workspace principal by verifying the `WorkspaceShare` capability in the `flows-sync-workspace` header; a header that is malformed, forged, expired, or signed by an unknown key is refused outright rather than downgraded to anonymity. A run mapped to a shared branch is visible only under a `BranchShare` capability, and without one every branch run is closed. Both capabilities are HMAC-SHA-256 signatures over a length-prefixed encoding of their claims, led by a scheme label so one cannot be replayed as the other. Secrets are `Redacted`, and a `kid` lets keys rotate without invalidating capabilities minted under a retired one. A subscription is authorized once, when it opens, and ends with `unauthorized` when the signed expiry arrives, because a stream that stayed connected would otherwise outlive its credential.

## Why followership fits dashboards and auditors

A dashboard or an auditor needs the whole truth and zero authority. Followership is exactly that shape: the follower sees everything its principal covers and can affect nothing. A follower that is slow, wrong, or compromised cannot mutate a run, hold a lease, or block a producer; its worst outcome is stale output. Every fan-out surface is bounded, so one follower's cost is a function of the configured bound rather than of the workspace's size or of how far behind it has fallen. Change feeds slide rather than block, so a stalled subscriber costs itself latency and never grows the publisher.

## Trade-offs

Server responses are admitted, never trusted. A frame that carries another run's entry, repeats or reorders a sequence, or serves an entry at or below the cursor is refused as a `protocol_violation` before any cursor moves.

- The frame ceiling (default 1 MiB) is a budget on one page, not a verdict on the read: a page that would cross it reports `done: false`, and only a single entry larger than the ceiling fails `frame_too_large`.
- One page is shared across the runs it covers, so a run with a backlog takes the larger part but never all of it, and a bootstrapping follower reaches the runs behind a busy one.
- The `Heartbeat` frame is reserved and no server emits one at 1.0.0-rc.0: keepalive is a transport concern, because a heartbeat here would spend the subscription's credit.
- A resync moves a cursor, not state. The wire carries no checkpoint state, so a follower with derived state restores the compacted prefix out of band before the cursor moves.

## Related

- [Sync followers](/docs/guides/sync-followers/): run a follower process against a workspace.
- [Durable execution](/docs/concepts/durable-execution/): the journal the wire replicates.
- [Retention](/docs/guides/retention/): compaction and what a follower does when history is deleted.
- [Observability](/docs/guides/observability/): projections and exports built on the same record.

# The agent runtime
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/agent-runtime/

Most of Smithers is mechanism: journal, engine, stores, sync. `@smthrs/agent` is where that mechanism becomes an agent. It is one service, `Agent`, whose single method runs one whole cell loop on the durable engine, plus the two adapters that embed the loop: `AgentSession` runs it as a control-plane run, and `AgentAction` runs it as one typed step inside a larger flow.

## The cell loop

A frame is: model, cell, realm evaluation, durable flow calls, transition. A cell is the JavaScript program the model emits for that frame. It evaluates in a QuickJS sandbox inside one persistent realm per run, so a name bound in frame 3 is still bound in frame 9 and a cell reads what earlier cells built instead of re-deriving it. A cell's only authority is `ctx.call(flowName, input)`: there is no `ctx.fs`, no `ctx.shell`, no `ctx.mcp`. Every capability a cell reaches is an ordinary flow settling through its own keyed, journaled, permission-gated boundary. A crash or a park mid-cell re-executes the cell source from the top, replays the boundaries that already settled, and reaches the parked call deterministically.

```ts



const Research = AgentAction.make("docs/Research", {
  payload: { topic: Schema.String },
  output: Schema.Struct({ summary: Schema.String }),
  seat: "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",
  system: ["You are a research assistant."],
  prompt: ({ topic }) => `Research ${topic}.`
})
```

## Two adapters, one loop

`AgentSession` is the production `ControlExecutor`: a launch accepted by the control plane becomes one durable flow execution whose id is the control run id, its events go to the journal, and an operator steers and approves it. `AgentAction` declares an ordinary action (same tag, same payload schema, same durable replay) whose implementation is the loop, bounded by a declared output schema that is rendered into the run's teaching and enforced against its final answer. Neither adapter reimplements the loop. An agent that drives a foreign CLI would be another implementation of `Agent.Service`, not a second loop beside this one.

## Seats and seat resolution

A seat has two halves that live in different places on purpose. The declared half is an ordinary string: what a markdown flow's `model:` frontmatter carries and what `AgentAction`'s `seat` option takes. It holds no credentials, no endpoint, and no client. `provider:modelId` such as `anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5` is the convention the Node CLI resolver understands, not a rule the agent enforces. The resolved half, `Seat.Seat`, is the only thing `Agent.run` accepts: a live model, the route resolver that seals its requests, and the model's context window in tokens so compaction has a real budget. `SeatResolver` is the credentialed seam between them. The CLI installs a resolver that reads keys from the environment; a test installs one that answers with a scripted model and never touches the network. A seat the host cannot serve is a typed `Seat.SeatUnresolved`, not a run that fails halfway through.

## CellPlugin hooks

Extensibility is a plugin kernel with waterfall hooks at the points where a decision is still reversible:

- `cellRegistry` transforms the one registry used for disclosure and call resolution.
- `cellFlows` adds or transforms executable flow bindings: the array the last handler returns is both the catalog the model is shown and what the call boundary resolves against, so a plugin contributes capabilities, not descriptions of them.
- `cellModelRequest` transforms the provider-neutral request immediately before its sealed model step.

`CellPlugin.fromBindings` authors the common case, a plugin that contributes bindings, with no hook knowledge. `configResolved` is a nonfatal observer boundary: a failed observer logs one warning with its stable code and never fails the composition.

## Where the runtime sits

`@smthrs/harness` owns the engine port (`sealStep`, `call`, `record`, `suspend`, and the rest) and deliberately depends on no engine, so the browser bundle never pulls in the durable engine. `@smthrs/agent` ships `FlowEngineLike`, the port's implementation over `@smthrs/engine`, and composes the harness controller, the QuickJS sandbox, registry-backed call resolution, and the plugin kernel around it. What comes back from `Agent.run` is a framework-neutral `Stream<AgentEvent>`: a caller renders it, journals it, or ignores it.

## What the runtime owns and what the model owns

The runtime owns identity, durability, and policy. `sealStep` digests the credential-free prepared request together with declared key material into a step key; credentials are signed on after the digest and never enter it, so a replayed turn re-emits the recorded model events instead of paying the provider again, and a provider wire change re-keys the step. The runtime also owns budgets (`Sandbox.Limits` per cell, `maxFrames` per loop, `Budget` per run), quota parks, and authorization, which is checked before a boundary opens because an activity's outcome is journaled.

The model owns the cells: what to compute, which flows to call, and when to declare `ctx.done`. What it can see is the projected `ctx.flows` catalog and nothing else, and the catalog is a contract: the declaration digest a cell was written against is re-derived at the call boundary, so a declaration that moved between disclosure and dispatch is refused rather than run against a body the model never saw. The runtime never writes a cell; the model never touches the journal. The provider-tool-call loop is gone, and nothing replaced it beside the cell path.

## Related

- [First agent flow](/docs/tutorials/first-agent-flow/): run the loop end to end.
- [Model seats](/docs/guides/model-seats/): how declared seats resolve to credentialed models.
- [Agent policies](/docs/guides/agent-policies/): quotas, budgets, and correction ladders.
- [Durable execution](/docs/concepts/durable-execution/): the engine underneath the loop.

# Memory
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/memory/

A run's journal records what the run did. It does not record what the agent learned, and a flow that runs twice starts knowing nothing unless something carries knowledge across runs. `@smthrs/memory` is that something: durable, cross-run storage for facts, conversation history, and notes, with a recall seam a host can rebind and maintenance effects a scheduler can run.

## What the store holds

`MemoryStore` is the authoritative contract, backed by SQL. It holds three record families: facts (JSON values under keys, with provenance, tags, and optional time-to-live), threads and their messages (the history family), and notes (reviewable text with a status; `listNotes` shows accepted notes unless you ask for another status). Two callable flows sit on top. `Flows.remember` writes one record and declares the `irreversible` tier because it writes. `Flows.recall` reads advisory rows and declares `sealed`, so it nests inside a sealed or compensable envelope without widening its tier.

## Namespaces and policies

Every record lives in a namespace: a kind (`flow`, `agent`, `user`, or `global`) plus an id. The kind is a stable lifetime. A bank is the public spelling of a namespace: an unprefixed bank is flow-local, a prefix such as `flow-` or `global-` names an explicit lifetime, and `Bank.parse` rejects an empty or malformed bank with `invalid_namespace`. Because `bank` and `flow-bank` resolve to the same namespace, recall de-duplicates on the resolved namespace rather than on the bank string.

A delegated plan generates work its author never named, so memory settings attach to the flow tree instead of threading through every call. `WithMemory.withMemory(flow, policy)` returns a copy of the flow carrying one policy of `namespace`, `recall` (`"auto"` or `"none"`), `maxTokens`, and `retain` (`"on-complete"` or `"never"`), and gives the same policy to every flow that flow declares.

```ts


const scoped = WithMemory.withMemory(Flows.recall, {
  namespace: { kind: "flow", id: "release-notes" },
  recall: "auto",
  maxTokens: 2048,
  retain: "on-complete"
})
```

A policy supplies defaults and never overrides: a caller that names its own banks or its own budget keeps them. Two values are refusals, not defaults. `recall: "none"` returns no rows and never reaches the recall service. `retain: "never"` drops the write while the caller still receives the key it asked for. The policy is an annotation: it takes no part in flow identity, so applying one never changes the graph a flow plans, node for node.

`MemoryTrellis.make` is the delegation case. A model-authored plan fills its leaf slots at run time, so a leaf cannot be handed a namespace at declaration time; `MemoryTrellis.make` applies one policy to the plan author, to the leaf, and to the memory flows those declare, then annotates the trellis itself. The graph stays the plain trellis graph, node for node.

## Recall strategies and when each fits

`Recall` is a replaceable seam, and the package ships three bindings.

`RecallKeyword` has no host dependencies and normalizes both query and row text to NFKC before matching. It fits tests, browsers, and stores that have not opted into full text search. `RecallFts` is the SQLite FTS5 binding: a namespace kind must opt in through `enableFts`, a query against a kind that has not fails with `fts_not_enabled`, and it fits the durable SQL store once the volume makes row scans expensive. The two can disagree on compatibility-equivalent characters, because FTS5 does not normalize to NFKC. `RecallSemantic` is in-process vector recall with an opt-in, best-effort projection through `decorateStore`: the authoritative store writes no embedding vectors on its own, and recall only lists vectors written under the model it was asked for. It fits questions where paraphrase matters more than exact terms and an embedding provider is available.

## Maintenance

Maintenance is a set of finite effects meant for explicit schedules, not a background daemon. `Maintenance.ttlGc` removes an expired fact together with its full-text projection and its vector rows in one transaction. `Maintenance.limitHistory` bounds history against a token budget, and `Maintenance.compact` summarizes old material down.

## Behaviors worth knowing

- Fact values are stored as JSON, serialized once at API entry: `NaN` and `Infinity` come back as `null`, and the stored JSON, the search text, the retained tags, and any vector projection all come from that one snapshot.
- A message id is unique within its thread, not globally; a same-thread retry whose creation data differs fails `idempotency_conflict` with a path to the first differing field.
- `appendMessage` creates a missing thread in the `global` namespace under the id `history`, so call `createThread` first when the thread belongs somewhere else.
- A read `limit` bounds the rows you receive after every status, supersession, and tag-group filter, so a bounded read never under-fills while matching rows remain.

## Boundaries

Memory is not a cache. A cache is disposable and its loss is invisible; memory is authoritative state with provenance and namespaces, and losing it changes what later runs know. Memory is not a vector store you manage by hand: the semantic projection is derivative and opt-in, and the store of record stays facts, messages, and notes. Recall is advisory: it answers rows within a budget, and a policy refusal wins over what the caller asked for. `maxTokens` is a UTF-8 byte ceiling over the serialized result array, not a tokenizer's count, because bytes conservatively bound tokens without committing the package to one model's tokenizer.

## Related

- [Memory tutorial](/docs/tutorials/memory/): remember and recall across two runs.
- [Memory operations](/docs/guides/memory-ops/): policies, maintenance schedules, and store care.
- [The agent runtime](/docs/concepts/agent-runtime/): where memory plugs into the cell loop.

# Why Effect
https://smithers.sh/docs/concepts/why-effect/

Smithers is a durable-execution engine built on Effect. That is a load-bearing choice, not a style one: the journal, the retry model, the test story, and the package boundaries all come out of what Effect gives a flow program.

## Flows are Effect programs

A flow body is a pure function that returns an Effect, and an action is an Effect with declared payload, success, and error schemas. The engine interprets the program, and every side effect the program performs is journaled as it happens, so a crashed process resumes from the record. Errors are typed: the failure channel of a step is a union the compiler checks, and a retry policy can branch on it instead of parsing messages.

## Layers, not hooks

An implementation attaches to a declaration as a layer, and a composition is layers merged and provided. `Greet.toLayer` supplies an action's code, `Interpreter.layer` drives a flow's body, `FlowEngine.layerMemory` or the SQLite engine store supplies the runtime, and `Layer.mergeAll` with `Layer.provideMerge` wires the stack. There is no global registry and no hook list to mutate. Swapping the engine layer moves a flow, source unchanged, from an in-memory engine to a durable one.

```ts







const Greet = Action.make("examples/Greet", {
  payload: { name: Schema.String },
  success: Schema.String
})

const Greeting = Flow.make("examples/Greeting", {
  payload: { name: Schema.String },
  success: Schema.String,
  body: (payload) => Greet.call(payload)
})

const GreetingLayer = Layer.mergeAll(
  Greet.toLayer(({ name }) => Effect.succeed(`Hello, ${name}.`)),
  Interpreter.layer(Greeting)
).pipe(
  Layer.provideMerge(Action.layerImplementations),
  Layer.provideMerge(FlowEngine.layerMemory),
  Layer.provideMerge(NodeCrypto.layer)
)
```

Because behavior is context, a test provides a different context: the same flow runs against an in-memory engine, a scripted model, or a stubbed clock, with no edits to the flow source and no module mocking. That is what the feature list means by "Layers, not hooks."

## The FlowRuntime port

`@smthrs/flow` declares `FlowRuntime`, the port the authoring APIs are written against: registration, execution, polling, interruption, resume, deferred lookup and completion, and clock scheduling. The package depends on nothing that implements it. The dependency direction is `@smthrs/flow`, then `@smthrs/engine`, then the durable stores, with no cycle and no type-only escape hatch back. That direction is what lets the whole authoring surface bundle for the browser: durability arrives with whichever runtime you provide.

## The pinned version and what it buys

Effect is pinned to exactly `4.0.0-rc.108`, and a project must resolve one Effect instance. Schema internals are not interoperable between two instances, so a project with two copies would decode the same journal payload two different ways. The pin buys one schema universe: a value encoded in one process decodes identically in every other process of the project, which is what a shared journal and a shared step cache require.

On top of the pin, the engine uses three Effect guarantees everywhere. Typed errors: a step's failure channel is declared and checked, so quarantine and retry decisions branch on structure. Testable layers: any credentialed or environmental piece is swapped at composition time. Structured concurrency: a run is a scope, cancellation propagates at once, and only an interrupt explicitly marked as infrastructure consumes a retry policy.

Effect is not an interchangeable detail. The pin is a hard requirement of the project layout, not a recommendation. [Installation](/docs/installation/) carries the pin mechanics, including why `@effect/platform-node-shared` is named on the install line, and [Effect version drift](/docs/troubleshooting/effect-version-drift/) covers the failure mode when the tree drifts.

## Where Smithers diverges from upstream

Effect ships a workflow package of its own. Smithers vendors that surface rather than depending on it, then diverges by being stricter and more cacheable. Upstream derives a run's identity by hashing the flow tag and payload, so unrelated runs with equal payloads silently join; here the caller chooses the execution id and derivation is opt-in. Upstream derives a step's identity from its activity's name, so renaming an activity corrupts replay; here step keys are content-addressed over canonical JSON. Upstream retries any interruption ten times by default; here cancellation propagates at once.

## Related

- [Installation](/docs/installation/): the pinned install line and repair commands.
- [Effect version drift](/docs/troubleshooting/effect-version-drift/): diagnose a second Effect instance in the tree.
- [Durable execution](/docs/concepts/durable-execution/): what the journaled program buys you.
- [Module flows](/docs/guides/module-flows/): the authoring surface these layers serve.

# Library API
https://smithers.sh/docs/reference/api/

The Smithers library is a roster of `@smthrs/*` packages, each with one reference page here.

## Install

The pinned install line for a library project:

```bash
pnpm add @smthrs/flow@next @smthrs/engine@next effect@4.0.0-rc.108 @effect/platform-node@4.0.0-rc.108 @effect/platform-node-shared@4.0.0-rc.108
```

The `@next` suffix is required: release candidates publish to the `next` dist-tag, and `latest` still resolves the Smithers 0.x line. Effect is pinned to exactly `4.0.0-rc.108`. For the `smithers` command, install `npm install --global @smthrs/cli@next`.

## Reading these pages

Each page is stitched from the package's colocated `docs/api.md`: the source of truth lives beside the code, and the generated page republishes it. `internal/*` is never public, and neither are nested `*/index` subpaths. Every documented namespace is also importable as a subpath of its package (for example `@smthrs/cli/<Module>` beside `@smthrs/cli`).

# @smthrs/flow
https://smithers.sh/docs/reference/api/flow/

Install the package and the exact `effect` version it pins:

```bash
pnpm add @smthrs/flow@next effect@4.0.0-rc.108
```

## Entry points

The `exports` map declares these subpaths:

| Import | Source | Platform |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@smthrs/flow` | `src/index.ts` | any |
| `@smthrs/flow/Action` | `src/Action/index.ts` | any |
| `@smthrs/flow/CacheEnvironment` | `src/Action/CacheEnvironment.ts` | any |
| `@smthrs/flow/FileBoundary` | `src/Action/FileBoundary.ts` | any |

| `@smthrs/flow/FlowRuntime` | `src/FlowRuntime/index.ts` | any |
| `@smthrs/flow/StepIdentity` | `src/Action/StepIdentity.ts` | any |
| `@smthrs/flow/<Module>` | `src/<Module>.ts` | any |

The `./*` subpath covers the top-level modules (`DurableClock`, `DurableDeferred`, `DurableQueue`, `Graph`, `HumanTask`, `Interpreter`, `Poll`, `RetryPolicy`, `Sleep`, `WaitFor`). The `exports` map maps `./internal/*`, `./*/index`, `./Action/*`, `./Flow/*`, and `./FlowRuntime/*` to `null`, so those paths do not resolve.

## Namespaces

The package index re-exports fourteen namespaces:

| Namespace | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| `Action` | Durable action definitions and combinators. |
